profiles.name: Ellen Grady
profiles.description: Ellen Grady, daughter of Camden 28 defendant John Grady and sister of Clare and Teresa Grady, was an aide to an elderly woman and peace worker in Ithaca, NY at the time of Plowshares Number Four. She and her husband Peter DeMott (Plowshares Number Two) helped establish the Ithaca Catholic Worker community in the 1990s and have continued lifelong nonviolent resistance, including organizing against drone-warfare operations at Hancock Air Force Base. Peter DeMott died in a fall in 2009.

profiles.name: Russell Ford
profiles.description: First New Englander since the U.S. war in Indochina to be indicted for nonregistration. Arrested for refusal to register on Aug. 10, 1982 in Hartford, Connecticut. At his arrest a fellow resister hugged him in solidarity, prompting federal marshals to charge that resister with "assaulting federal officers by embracing Russell Ford." One of the "imprisoned nine" who served federal time.
profiles.finding: Militant4636 identifies Hartford draft resister; no captioned portrait established.

profiles.name: Richard Cleaver
profiles.description: Richard Cleaver was an Iowa writer, Catholic Worker activist, and theologian. A 1975 graduate of Grinnell College, he later wrote New Heaven, New Earth about the Catholic Worker program and Know My Name, which approached gay liberation through liberation theology. Cleaver was arrested after returning to Offutt Air Force Base during the Nagasaki Day peace action on August 9, 1982 despite an earlier barring letter. He was sentenced to probation on December 14, 1982; no prison term was imposed.
profiles.finding: Sower winter2025 memorial matches Grinnell1975 Catholic Worker and includes singing photo; stable source/asset needed. Smithsonian ceramic artist namesake rejected.

profiles.name: David Alan Wayte
profiles.description: Former Yale philosophy student from Pasadena who wrote letters to government officials publicly announcing his refusal to register; the letters were placed in a Selective Service file used by DOJ to select "vocal" nonregistrants for prosecution. Indicted July 22, 1982. U.S. District Judge Terry Hatter dismissed the indictment on selective-prosecution grounds; the Supreme Court reversed in Wayte v. United States, 470 U.S. 598 (1985), 7-2, holding that DOJ's selective prosecution did not violate the First or Fifth Amendments. Wayte then pleaded guilty in June 1985 and Hatter sentenced him on Sept. 10, 1985 to six months under house arrest at his grandmother's home — far below the 5-year statutory maximum.
profiles.finding: LA Times1985 and Justia710F2d1385 identity evidence; no individual portrait.

profiles.name: Tim Quinn
profiles.description:
House painter from Hartford, CT; took part in the 1982 Trident Nein action aboard the USS Florida at Electric Boat, Groton, CT, boarding the submarine by canoe and hammering on missile hatches.

Tim Quinn was 28 at the time of Trident Nein, an expectant father working as a house painter in Hartford, Connecticut. No further sourceable biographical detail was found.
profiles.finding: Pax Christi2022 Trident Nein retrospective lead. NIST pacemaker and Commons Tim Quinn not independently matched.

profiles.name: Bill Hartman
profiles.description: Bill Hartman was a Philadelphia peace worker associated with the Atlantic Life Community. On July 5, 1982, he joined the Trident Nein Plowshares action at the General Dynamics Electric Boat shipyard in Groton, Connecticut. Hartman, James Cunningham, Vincent Kay, and Tim Quinn reached the USS Florida by canoe, hammered on missile hatches, poured blood, and renamed the submarine “USS Auschwitz.” Police arrested the group at the shipyard. A jury convicted all nine participants of criminal mischief, conspiracy, and criminal trespass, and Hartman received a jail sentence on November 9, 1982.
profiles.finding: Pax Christi2022 Trident Nein action corroboration; Getty football player Bill Hartman rejected.

profiles.name: James Cunningham
profiles.description: James Cunningham, 40 at the time of Trident Nein, was a former lawyer who had given up a high-living legal practice (and a house in Laguna Beach, California) to join the Jonah House resistance community in Baltimore founded by Phil Berrigan and Liz McAlister. He had previously served 60 days for trespassing at the Trident submarine plant in Bangor, Washington, before joining Jonah House through his friend Karl Smith.

profiles.name: Vincent Kay

profiles.name: Karl Zanzig
profiles.description: Karl Zanzig was a Montana anti-nuclear activist associated with the Species Life community and Silence One Silo. On June 5, 1982, Zanzig and Mark Anderlik entered the Romeo-29 Minuteman missile silo near Conrad, Montana, scattered wheat seeds, and shared bread. After two days in pretrial custody, Zanzig served a later prison term at Lompoc Federal Prison Camp from September 13, 1982 to January 24, 1983.

profiles.name: Wade E. Roberts
profiles.description: Wade E. Roberts was a U.S. Army private stationed in West Germany who went absent without leave on March 2, 1987. Roberts and his West German partner reached East Germany, and the Soviet Union granted them political asylum. Soviet authorities settled them in Ashkhabad, in the Turkmen Soviet republic. Roberts said he had sought asylum after harassment in the Army, although the record located does not tie his action to opposition to a particular war. He returned to West Germany on November 3, 1987 to face military proceedings. A court-martial later cleared him of desertion and convicted him of the lesser AWOL offense.

profiles.name: John Frank Cardiello
profiles.description: John Frank Cardiello, known as Frank, was a Catholic Worker organizer, psychiatric nurse practitioner, and peace activist. While studying theology at Creighton University, he helped organize the Omaha Catholic Worker House men’s shelter and community kitchen and coordinated food donations for its programs. Cardiello entered Offutt Air Force Base during the Feast of the Holy Innocents peace witness on December 28, 1981. Military authorities detained him for several hours, issued a barring letter, and released him that day. He later earned nursing degrees and practiced geriatric psychiatric nursing in Helena, Montana. He died March 30, 2006.

profiles.name: Sister Joyce Horbach
profiles.description: Sister Joyce Horbach, born Coletta Horbach on March 23, 1916, was a member of the Sisters of St. Francis of Dubuque and a longtime peace-and-justice activist. Horbach returned for the August 9, 1982 Nagasaki Day action and received probation. Her Franciscan community later remembered six arrests and her continuing participation in peace demonstrations, including annual School of the Americas protests. She died March 5, 2015.

After October 1981 Bronx apartment FBI raid federal charges were dropped due to COINTELPRO illegality. profiles.name: Norberto Cintrón Fiallo
profiles.description: Norberto Cintrón Fiallo was a Puerto Rican independence militant and a leader of the Armed Forces of Popular Resistance (Fuerzas Armadas de Resistencia Popular, FARP). In the early 1980s he was subpoenaed by federal grand juries in New York investigating the Puerto Rican independence movement and was ordered to provide hair samples and testimony. Refusing to recognize the authority of the grand jury, he declined to cooperate. A first grand jury impaneled in 1980 was dissolved without holding him in contempt; a second then jailed him for civil contempt. He served roughly eighteen months in prison, from 1984 to 1985, before a judge ordered his release. A longtime organizer for Puerto Rican independence and a board member of the anti-repression committee CUCRE, Cintrón Fiallo remained active in the movement until his death in 2024.

She later directed the Livermore Action Group and co-founded the Spirit affinity group with her then-husband Terry Messman. In April 1983 she joined a Good Friday blockade at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory and was released on a citation.

She later joined the 1985 Martin Marietta MX Witness action and became an artist-in-residence with RAWtools, which turns donated guns into garden tools.

profiles.name: Vince Scotti Eirene

He later founded the Duncan Porter House of Hospitality and Resistance, provided housing and support to unhoused people, and took part in antiwar, environmental, and nuclear-disarmament campaigns. He died September 11, 2025 at age 73.

profiles.name: Allen Blitz
profiles.description:
Allen Blitz — a marcher who returned fire as the Klansmen and Nazis opened fire — was one of the Communist Workers Party anti-Klan demonstrators charged with rioting after the November 3, 1979 Greensboro Massacre — the attack in which Ku Klux Klansmen and American Nazis shot and killed five CWP activists at a "Death to the Klan" march in Greensboro, North Carolina. In a striking inversion of justice, the gunmen were acquitted by all-white juries while the wounded and surviving demonstrators were the ones prosecuted. The rioting charges against the demonstrators were dropped in November 1980.

His jailing can be dated from a contemporary Workers Viewpoint report: he was arrested on May 2, 1980, after the felony-riot indictments came down — not at the massacre itself — and was still in jail on May 3 with his wife Dori and Lacie Russell after Nelson Johnson and Rand Manzella posted bond. On May 5 a judge reduced the remaining defendants' bail to $5,000 each, apparently permitting their release, making his time jailed approximately three days.
profiles.finding: UNCG Greensboro archive and City of Two TalesPDF provide event evidence; no individual caption/crop established.

profiles.name: Seamus Moley
profiles.description:
Seamus Moley was an Irish national swept into a series of U.S. investigations targeting alleged IRA-linked arms procurement operations. The underlying allegations reflected a strategic focus on anti-aircraft capability—weaponry intended to threaten British military aircraft—rather than small-arms shipments alone.

Moley was arrested in January 1990 in the same Stinger-missile undercover operation that ensnared McKinley and others. He later entered a plea agreement in March 1995 on arms-smuggling charges and was sentenced to 19 months in federal prison in June 1995. He was released from custody and deported to Ireland in July 1996.
profiles.finding: Footage.net Stinger prosecution video and LA Times1990 identity context; no individual verified still.

profiles.name: Andrew Duggan
profiles.description: Andrew Duggan was an Irish-American supporter of Irish republicanism who lived in New City, New York, and was active in the Irish Northern Aid Committee. Federal agents arrested him on June 21, 1982 during an investigation of a plan to buy and export weapons, including surface-to-air missiles and rifles, for the Provisional Irish Republican Army. He was released on a $50,000 personal-recognizance bond. After a nine-week federal trial in Brooklyn, a jury convicted Duggan in May 1983 of conspiracy and several weapons-transport and export offenses. The court imposed concurrent terms, the longest of which was three years. The United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit upheld the convictions in 1984.
